source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 16 (PDF 61-84, printed 1-24); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 16 (Electrostatics / Static Electricity), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Electrostatics deals with the phenomena arising from:
blocks.explanation: Electrostatics (static electricity) refers to phenomena arising from stationary charges (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Electrostatics or static electricity refers to the phenomena arising from the stationary electric charges

blocks.prompt: 2 The direction of the electrostatic force between two charges depends on:

options.text: the nature of the charges (positive or negative)

blocks.explanation: The direction of the Coulomb force depends on whether the charges are positive or negative (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: The direction of this force depends on the nature of charges whether positive or negative

blocks.prompt: 3 Electric potential difference between two points is the:

options.text: work done per unit charge in moving a charge between them
force per unit charge at a point

blocks.explanation: Potential difference V = W_AB/q₀: work done per unit charge between two points (16.1).

book_ref.quote: The electric potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between two points

blocks.prompt: 4 One volt is equal to:

book_ref.quote: The SI unit is the volt, where

blocks.prompt: 5 In E = −ΔV/Δd, the negative sign shows that the electric field points:

options.text: towards the negative of distance only

blocks.explanation: The minus sign indicates the field points from higher to lower potential (16.1).

book_ref.quote: Where the negative sign indicates that the field points from higher to lower potential

blocks.prompt: 6 The electric field intensity at a point is equal to the negative of:

options.text: the rate of change of potential with time
the rate of change of potential with distance
the product of potential and distance
the potential energy per unit mass

blocks.explanation: E = −ΔV/Δd: the field is the (negative) rate of change of potential with distance (16.1).

book_ref.quote: the electric field represents the rate of change of potential with distance

blocks.prompt: 7 On moving along the direction of a uniform electric field, the electric potential:
blocks.explanation: With the corrected sign, ΔV = −E Δd: the potential decreases in the direction of the field (16.1, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: the potential decreases in the direction of the field

blocks.prompt: 8 For the same distance, a stronger uniform electric field gives:
blocks.explanation: For a uniform field V = Ed, so a stronger field causes a more rapid decrease in potential (16.1).

book_ref.quote: a stronger electric field causes a more rapid decrease in potential

blocks.prompt: 9 A 12 V battery is connected across two parallel plates 0.4 cm apart. The electric field between the plates is:

book_ref.quote: In the case of a uniform electric field, this relation simplifies to:

blocks.prompt: 10 Two points 2 mm apart lie along a uniform field of 5000 N C⁻¹. The potential difference between them is:

book_ref.quote: Showing that the potential difference between two points is directly proportional to the electric field strength

blocks.prompt: 11 Work of 3 × 10⁻⁴ J is done in moving a charge of 6 μC between two points. The potential difference between them is:

book_ref.quote: The electric potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between two points

blocks.prompt: 12 In practice, the absolute value of electric potential at a point is measured with respect to:
blocks.explanation: Though infinity is taken at zero potential, practically the Earth is assumed to be at zero potential (16.1, box).

book_ref.quote: the Earth is assumed to be at zero potential practically

blocks.prompt: 13 The reference point of zero electric potential for a point charge is usually taken:
blocks.explanation: The zero-potential reference is usually taken at infinity (16.2).

book_ref.quote: we must have a reference to which we assign zero electric potential. This point is usually taken at infinity

blocks.prompt: 14 Electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge:

options.text: from that point to infinity with acceleration
from infinity to that point in equilibrium
from the Earth to that point with acceleration

blocks.explanation: Potential = work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to the point, keeping it in equilibrium (16.2).

book_ref.quote: The electric potential at any point in an electric field is equal to work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity

blocks.prompt: 15 Electric potential is a scalar quantity because:

options.text: both work and charge are scalars

blocks.explanation: V = W/q₀ and both W and q₀ are scalars (16.2).

book_ref.quote: Both potential and potential differences are scalar quantities because both W and q

blocks.prompt: 16 ΔV = −E Δr cannot be used directly over a large distance from a point charge because:

options.text: E is zero near the charge
E varies inversely as the square of distance

blocks.explanation: Near a point charge E ∝ 1/r², so E is not constant and basic principles are used (16.2).

book_ref.quote: However in this case E varies inversely as square of distance from the point charge

blocks.prompt: 17 In deriving the potential of a point charge, for points A and B very close together, r² is replaced by:
blocks.explanation: Taking arithmetic mean ≈ geometric mean gives r² = r_A r_B (Eq. 16.11).

book_ref.quote: we can take the arithmetic mean to be equal to geometric mean

blocks.prompt: 18 The absolute potential at distance r from a point charge q is:
blocks.explanation: Putting V_B = 0 at infinity gives V = (1/4πε₀)(q/r) (Eqs. 16.16-16.17).

book_ref.quote: To calculate absolute potential or potential at A, point B is assumed to be infinity point

blocks.prompt: 19 If the distance from a point charge is doubled, the electric potential becomes:
blocks.explanation: V ∝ 1/r (Eq. 16.17), so doubling r halves V.

book_ref.quote: The general expression for electric potential

blocks.prompt: 20 The electric potential at a point 0.9 m from a charge of 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ C is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):

book_ref.quote: Find the electric potential at a point 1.2 m from a charge

blocks.prompt: 21 The potential at 30 cm from a charge of −3 nC is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):
blocks.explanation: V = (9 × 10⁹)(−3 × 10⁻⁹)/0.30 = −90 V; it is negative for a negative charge (16.2).

book_ref.quote: The electric potential will be negative if the charge q is negative

blocks.prompt: 22 The total electric potential at a point due to several charges is:

options.text: the vector sum of the individual potentials
the algebraic sum of the individual potentials
the product of the individual potentials

blocks.explanation: Potential is a scalar; the total is the algebraic sum of individual potentials (16.2).

book_ref.quote: the total electric potential is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials created by all the charges

blocks.prompt: 23 Charges of +2 nC and +3 nC are each 0.3 m from a point P. The total potential at P is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):

book_ref.quote: the total electric potential is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials created by all the charges

blocks.prompt: 24 Charges +9 μC and −3 μC are 40 cm apart. The zero-potential point between them is at a distance from the +9 μC charge of:
blocks.explanation: 9/x = 3/(40 − x) gives 360 − 9x = 3x, x = 30 cm (closer to the smaller negative charge, 16.2).

book_ref.quote: so there will be two zero potential points. Both the points should be closer to the smaller negative charge

blocks.prompt: 25 For the same charges (+9 μC and −3 μC, 40 cm apart), the zero-potential point outside them lies beyond the negative charge at:
blocks.explanation: 9/(40 + y) = 3/y gives 9y = 120 + 3y, y = 20 cm beyond the −3 μC charge (16.2).

book_ref.quote: so there will be two zero potential points. Both the points should be closer to the smaller negative charge

blocks.prompt: 26 When the first charge Q is brought from infinity to point A where there is no electric field, the work done is:
blocks.explanation: No field acts at A, so Q faces no opposition and W_A = 0 (Eq. 16.19).

book_ref.quote: Therefore, the work done to bring Q to point A is zero.

blocks.prompt: 27 The electric potential energy of two point charges Q and q separated by r is:

book_ref.quote: the work done in placing these two charges at points A and B is stored as electric potential energy

blocks.prompt: 28 Charges of 6 μC and 3 μC are 9.0 cm apart. Their electric potential energy is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):

book_ref.quote: Two point charges are separated by a distance of 4.0 cm.

blocks.prompt: 29 Charges of +4 μC and −2 μC are 0.2 m apart. Their electric potential energy is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):

book_ref.quote: The concept of electric potential directly leads to the expression for electric potential energy of two point charges

blocks.prompt: 30 If the separation of two point charges is made three times, their electric potential energy becomes:
blocks.explanation: E_p ∝ 1/r (Eq. 16.24), so tripling r gives one third of E_p.

book_ref.quote: Once the charge Q has been placed at point A, an electric potential V is created by it at point B.

blocks.prompt: 31 A charge of 2 μC is brought from infinity to a point where another charge has created a potential of 300 V. The work done is:

book_ref.quote: work has to be done in moving it against the electric filed

blocks.prompt: 32 A positive charge free to move in an electric field accelerates:
blocks.explanation: A free positive charge always accelerates from higher to lower potential (16.3).

book_ref.quote: it will always accelerate from a point of higher potential to a point of lower potential

blocks.prompt: 33 An electron released in an electric field moves:
blocks.explanation: A free negative charge moves from lower to higher potential (16.3).

book_ref.quote: A negative charge allowed to move freely in an electric field moves from a point of lower potential to a point of higher potential.

blocks.prompt: 34 When a free charge q₀ moves through a potential difference ΔV, the gain in its kinetic energy equals:
blocks.explanation: The decrease in potential energy ΔU = q₀ΔV appears as kinetic energy: ½mv² = q₀ΔV (Eq. 16.18).

book_ref.quote: This decrease in potential energy of the charge will appear as its kinetic energy.

blocks.prompt: 35 A particle of mass 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ kg carrying 5 μC starts from rest and moves through a potential difference of 100 V. Its final speed is:

book_ref.quote: the body will reach the point at lower potential energy with velocity v

blocks.prompt: 36 Electron-volt (eV) is a unit of:
blocks.explanation: The eV is a unit of energy used in atomic physics (16.3).

book_ref.quote: In atomic physics, we use one such unit of energy known as electron-volt (eV).

blocks.prompt: 37 One electron-volt is equal to:
blocks.explanation: 1 eV = charge on an electron × 1 volt = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (16.3).

book_ref.quote: It is the energy required by an electron which has been accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt.

blocks.prompt: 38 An electron accelerated from rest through 200 V gains kinetic energy of:

book_ref.quote: It is the energy required by an electron which has been accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt.

blocks.prompt: 39 An energy of 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁷ J expressed in electron-volts is:

book_ref.quote: The equation (16.18) suggests that the energy can also be expressed as the product of potential difference and charge.

blocks.prompt: 40 The two types of capacitors discussed in this chapter are:

options.text: isolated spherical conductors and parallel plate capacitors

blocks.explanation: 16.4 discusses (i) isolated spherical conductors and (ii) parallel plate capacitors.

book_ref.quote: We will discuss here two types of such devices.

blocks.prompt: 41 An isolated spherical conductor is one that is:

options.text: far from other conductors or influence

blocks.explanation: A sphere far from other conductors or influence is an isolated spherical conductor (16.4).

book_ref.quote: A spherical conductor placed in space such that it is far from other conductors or influence is known as an isolated spherical conductor

blocks.prompt: 42 The capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor is the:

options.text: charge stored per unit potential at its surface

blocks.explanation: C = Q/V: charge stored per unit potential at the surface (Eq. 16.25).

book_ref.quote: defined as the electric charge stored on the sphere per unit electric potential at its surface

blocks.prompt: 43 The capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius R in vacuum is:
blocks.explanation: Putting V = (1/4πε₀)(Q/R) in C = Q/V gives C = 4πε₀R (Eq. 16.26).

book_ref.quote: The electric potential V at the surface of the sphere of radius R is given by

blocks.prompt: 44 The capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius 9 cm is (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²):

book_ref.quote: the capacitance of a spherical conductor is independent of the charge or potential

blocks.prompt: 45 A sphere of capacitance 10 pF is raised to a surface potential of 3000 V. The charge on it is:

book_ref.quote: This means larger spheres store more charge at the same surface potential.

blocks.prompt: 46 If the radius of an isolated sphere is doubled, its capacitance becomes:
blocks.explanation: C = 4πε₀R, so C ∝ R; doubling R doubles C (16.4).

book_ref.quote: The capacitance increases with increase in radius of the sphere.

blocks.prompt: 47 An isolated sphere is placed in a medium of dielectric constant 3. Its capacitance compared with that in vacuum is:
blocks.explanation: C = 4πε₀εᵣR (Eq. 16.27), so εᵣ = 3 makes it three times.

book_ref.quote: However, the capacitance of a spherical conductor in a medium of dielectric constant

blocks.prompt: 48 On a charged isolated spherical conductor the charge resides:
blocks.explanation: On a conductor the charge lies on the outer surface (16.4, Book correction to Fig. 16.5).

book_ref.quote: On a conductor the charge lies on the outer surface

blocks.prompt: 49 For a spherical conductor, one farad is the capacitance of a sphere which stores:

options.text: 1 C at a potential of 1 kV
1 J at a potential of 1 V
1 C at a potential of 1 V
1 μC at a potential of 1 V

blocks.explanation: 1 farad = 1 coulomb/1 volt (16.4).

book_ref.quote: 1 farad is the capacitance of a sphere that stores 1 coulomb of charge when its electric potential is 1 volt

blocks.prompt: 50 A parallel plate capacitor consists of two conductors separated by:
blocks.explanation: The two plates are separated by vacuum, air or an insulator called a dielectric (16.5).

book_ref.quote: A parallel plate, capacitor consists of two conductors placed near one another separated by vacuum, air or any other insulator

blocks.prompt: 51 When a capacitor is connected to a battery, the two plates acquire:

options.text: unequal charges of the same sign

blocks.explanation: The plate joined to the positive terminal gets +Q and the other −Q (16.5).

book_ref.quote: the battery places a charge +Q on the plate connected with its positive terminal

blocks.prompt: 52 Capacitance is a measure of the ability of a capacitor to:
blocks.explanation: C is a measure of the ability of a capacitor to store charge (16.5).

book_ref.quote: It is a measure of the ability of capacitor to store charge.

blocks.prompt: 53 The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor does NOT depend on:
blocks.explanation: C depends on the geometry of the plates and the medium (16.5, Eq. 16.33), not on Q.

book_ref.quote: it depends upon the geometry of the plates and the medium between them

blocks.prompt: 54 The SI unit of capacitance, the farad, is equal to:
blocks.explanation: The SI unit of capacitance is coulomb per volt, called the farad (16.5).

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of capacitance is coulomb per volt

blocks.prompt: 55 The unit farad is named after:
blocks.explanation: Farad is named after the English scientist Michael Faraday (16.5).

book_ref.quote: after the famous English scientist Michael Faraday

blocks.prompt: 56 A 20 μF capacitor is connected to a 9 V battery. The charge on each plate is:

book_ref.quote: the amount of charge on one plate necessary to raise the potential of that plate by one volt with respect to the other

blocks.prompt: 57 The separation d of a parallel plate capacitor is kept small so that the field between the plates is:

options.text: uniform and confined between the plates

blocks.explanation: Small d keeps E uniform and almost entirely between the plates (16.5).

book_ref.quote: The distance d is small so that the electric field E between the plates is uniform

blocks.prompt: 58 The electric intensity between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor in vacuum is:
blocks.explanation: By Gauss's law, E = σ/ε₀ = Q/Aε₀ (Eq. 16.31).

book_ref.quote: As electric intensity between parallel plate capacitor (Gauss's law) is:

blocks.prompt: 59 The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with vacuum between its plates is:
blocks.explanation: C_vac = Q/V = Aε₀/d (Eq. 16.32).

book_ref.quote: Eq. (16.32) is for vacuum (or air)

blocks.prompt: 60 A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.02 m² separated by 1 mm of air. Its capacitance is (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²):

book_ref.quote: As electric intensity between parallel plate capacitor (Gauss's law) is:

blocks.prompt: 61 The same capacitor (0.02 m², 1 mm) is filled with a dielectric of εᵣ = 4. Its capacitance becomes (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²):

book_ref.quote: the capacitance of capacitor is enhanced by the factor

blocks.prompt: 62 If the separation between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is halved, its capacitance:
blocks.explanation: C = Aε₀/d, so C ∝ 1/d; halving d doubles C (Eq. 16.32).

book_ref.quote: Eq. (16.32) is for vacuum (or air)

blocks.prompt: 63 In the voltmeter experiment of Fig. 16.7, the deflection of the voltmeter connected across the capacitor plates measures the:
blocks.explanation: The deflection of the meter is a measure of the potential difference between the plates (16.5, Fig. 16.7).

book_ref.quote: When a dielectric material is inserted between the plates, reading drops indicating a decrease in the potential difference between the plates

blocks.prompt: 64 On inserting a dielectric into an isolated charged capacitor, which quantity remains constant?
blocks.explanation: Q remains constant while V decreases, so C = Q/V increases (16.5).

book_ref.quote: since V decreases while Q remains constant, the value of C increases

blocks.prompt: 65 A capacitor has capacitance 20 pF with vacuum and 90 pF with a dielectric between its plates. The dielectric constant is:

book_ref.quote: The ratio of the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with an insulating substance as medium between the plates

blocks.prompt: 66 The dielectric constant εᵣ of a medium has:
blocks.explanation: εᵣ = C_med/C_vac is a ratio of two capacitances, so it has no unit (Eq. 16.34).

book_ref.quote: Dividing Eq.16.33 by Eq.16.32, we get expression for dielectric constant as:

blocks.prompt: 67 The potential difference between the plates decreases on inserting a dielectric because of:

options.text: polarization of the atoms of the dielectric
leakage of charge to the Earth

blocks.explanation: The decrease is due to polarization of the atoms of the dielectric (16.5).

book_ref.quote: The reason for decrease in potential difference between the plates of the capacitor is the polarization of the atoms

blocks.prompt: 68 A dielectric is a material which:
blocks.explanation: A dielectric is an insulator; all its electrons are bound to their nuclei (16.5).

book_ref.quote: It has no free electrons, i.e., all the electrons are bound to their respective positively charged nuclei.

blocks.prompt: 69 When an atom of a dielectric is placed in an electric field, its electrons are displaced slightly:
blocks.explanation: Electrons shift slightly relative to the nucleus opposite to the field: polarization (16.5).

book_ref.quote: its electrons are displaced slightly relative to the nucleus in a direction opposite to the field

blocks.prompt: 70 The charges induced on the faces of a dielectric slab next to the capacitor plates are:

options.text: of the same sign as the adjacent plate
opposite in sign to the adjacent plate

blocks.explanation: The induced charges are opposite in polarity to the adjacent plate; this reduces E and V (16.5).

book_ref.quote: The polarity of these charges is opposite to that of the charge on the adjacent plate.

blocks.prompt: 71 Due to polarization of a dielectric between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor, the electric intensity between the plates:
blocks.explanation: The induced charges effectively reduce the charge, so E and V between the plates decrease (16.5).

book_ref.quote: Consequently, the electric intensity and potential difference between the plates decrease.

blocks.prompt: 72 Capacitors are combined in a circuit mainly to:

options.text: reduce the battery voltage to zero

blocks.explanation: Combination is done to obtain a desired capacitance (16.6).

book_ref.quote: It is done to obtain a desired capacitance.

blocks.prompt: 73 In a parallel combination of capacitors, the quantity that is the same for every capacitor is:
blocks.explanation: In parallel, V across each capacitor is the same; charges differ (16.6).

book_ref.quote: In this combination the potential difference V across the plates of each capacitor is the same.

blocks.prompt: 74 Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 5 μF are connected in parallel. The equivalent capacitance is:

book_ref.quote: When capacitors are connected in parallel, their combined capacitance is equal to the sum of their individual capacitances.

blocks.prompt: 75 Capacitors of 2 μF and 4 μF are connected in parallel across 12 V. The charge on the 4 μF capacitor is:
blocks.explanation: Same V in parallel: Q₂ = C₂V = 4 μF × 12 V = 48 μC (16.6).

book_ref.quote: The charge on each will be different depending upon its capacitance.

blocks.prompt: 76 A 60 pF capacitor charged to 50 V is joined in parallel to an uncharged capacitor; the common potential becomes 20 V. The capacitance of the second capacitor is:

book_ref.quote: As total charge remains constant, so charge shifted to

blocks.prompt: 77 In a series combination of capacitors, the quantity that is the same for every capacitor is:
blocks.explanation: In series each capacitor receives the same charge Q (by induction) (16.6).

book_ref.quote: Thus each capacitor receives a charge of magnitude Q on each of its plates.

blocks.prompt: 78 In a series combination, the second plate of the first capacitor gets its charge by:
blocks.explanation: The second plate is insulated from the first; +Q on the first plate induces −Q on it (16.6).

book_ref.quote: But the positive of the first plate induces an equal negative charge

blocks.prompt: 79 Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is:

book_ref.quote: The reciprocal of equivalent capacitance is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of individual capacitances

blocks.prompt: 80 Three equal capacitors of 6 μF each are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is:

book_ref.quote: The series combination is one after the other in a line.

blocks.prompt: 81 Capacitors of 6 μF and 3 μF in series are connected across 90 V. The potential difference across the 3 μF capacitor is:

book_ref.quote: In series combination charge on each capacitor will be the same Q.

blocks.prompt: 82 In a series combination, the largest potential difference appears across the capacitor of:

options.text: the capacitor nearest the positive terminal

blocks.explanation: Same Q in series and V = Q/C, so the smallest C has the largest V (16.6).

book_ref.quote: It will be different across each of them depending upon its capacitance.

blocks.prompt: 83 For three capacitors in series across a battery of voltage V:
blocks.explanation: In series the battery voltage is shared: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ (Eq. 16.36).

book_ref.quote: the potential difference across the combination of three capacitors is equal to that of battery terminals

blocks.prompt: 84 Compared with each individual capacitor, the equivalent capacitance of a parallel combination is:
blocks.explanation: C_e = C₁ + C₂ + C₃ is larger than any single capacitance (Eq. 16.35).

book_ref.quote: When capacitors are connected in parallel, their combined capacitance is equal to the sum of their individual capacitances.

blocks.prompt: 85 Compared with each individual capacitor, the equivalent capacitance of a series combination is:
blocks.explanation: 1/C_e = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃ makes C_e less than the smallest C (Eq. 16.37).

book_ref.quote: The reciprocal of equivalent capacitance is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of individual capacitances

blocks.prompt: 86 When the plates of a charged capacitor are joined by a thick wire, the wire becomes hot. This shows that:
blocks.explanation: The heat produced is the energy the charged capacitor possessed (16.7).

book_ref.quote: A good evidence of the energy stored in a charged capacitor is that of its discharging.

blocks.prompt: 87 For a capacitor, the graph of potential difference V against charge Q is:

options.text: a straight line through the origin

blocks.explanation: Q ∝ V, so the V-Q graph is a straight line through the origin (16.7, Fig. 16.10).

book_ref.quote: if we draw a V vs Q graph, it will be a straight line passing through the origin

blocks.prompt: 88 The energy stored in a charged capacitor is equal to the:
blocks.explanation: Total work = sum of rectangle areas = area under the V-Q graph (triangle OAB) (16.7).

book_ref.quote: this sum is equal to the total area under the graph

blocks.prompt: 89 The energy stored in a capacitor holding charge Q at potential difference V is:
blocks.explanation: Area of triangle OAB = ½(OA)(AB) = ½QV (Eq. 16.39).

book_ref.quote: If OA at this stage is equal to total charge Q and AB is equal to the final potential difference V then,

blocks.prompt: 90 A 10 μF capacitor is charged to 200 V. The energy stored in it is:

book_ref.quote: If we put the value of Q = CV in eq. (16.39), we get

blocks.prompt: 91 A capacitor holds 4 × 10⁻⁴ C at 50 V. The energy stored is:

book_ref.quote: If OA at this stage is equal to total charge Q and AB is equal to the final potential difference V then,

blocks.prompt: 92 If the potential difference across a capacitor is halved, the energy stored becomes:
blocks.explanation: W = ½CV² ∝ V², so halving V gives (½)² = ¼ of the energy (16.7).

book_ref.quote: doubling V increases the energy by a factor

blocks.prompt: 93 The energy density of an electric field E in a medium of relative permittivity εᵣ is:
blocks.explanation: Energy/volume = ½ε₀εᵣE² (Eq. 16.42).

book_ref.quote: It is also possible to regard the energy as being stored in electric field between the plates

blocks.prompt: 94 The energy density in air (εᵣ = 1) where the electric field is 2 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹ is (take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²):

book_ref.quote: This equation is valid for any electric field strength.

blocks.prompt: 95 In deriving the energy density of a parallel plate capacitor, the product Ad represents:
blocks.explanation: As (Ad) is the volume between the plates, energy/volume gives the energy density (16.7).

book_ref.quote: As (Ad) is the volume between the plates, so

blocks.prompt: 96 During charging, each next small increment of charge needs more work because:

options.text: the charge on the plates decreases
the potential difference between the plates keeps increasing

blocks.explanation: With each increment the potential difference rises, so more work is needed for the next increment (16.7).

book_ref.quote: a larger amount of work is needed to bring up next increment of charge

blocks.prompt: 97 Capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF in series are charged by a 60 V supply. The total energy stored is:

book_ref.quote: connected in series and charged by a 100V power supply

blocks.prompt: 98 The same capacitors (3 μF and 6 μF) are now connected in parallel to the 60 V supply. The total energy stored is:
blocks.explanation: C_e = 9 μF; W = ½(9 × 10⁻⁶)(60)² = 1.62 × 10⁻² J, more than in series (16.7).

book_ref.quote: connected in series and charged by a 100V power supply

blocks.prompt: 99 When an R-C circuit is connected to a battery V₀, the charge on the capacitor:
blocks.explanation: Charge builds up gradually from 0 to the equilibrium value q₀ = CV₀ (16.8).

book_ref.quote: The capacitor is not charged immediately, rather charges build up gradually to the equilibrium value

blocks.prompt: 100 If both the resistance and the capacitance of an R-C circuit are doubled, the time constant becomes:
blocks.explanation: The time constant is the product RC (16.8); 2R × 2C = 4RC.

book_ref.quote: depends upon the product of the resistance R and the capacitance C used in the circuit

blocks.prompt: 101 During charging, the time constant is the time in which the capacitor acquires:
blocks.explanation: Time constant: time to deposit 0.63 times the equilibrium charge q₀ (16.8).

book_ref.quote: defined as the time required by the capacitor to deposit 0.63 times the equilibrium charge

blocks.prompt: 102 The time constant of a circuit with R = 2 kΩ and C = 50 μF is:

book_ref.quote: As the unit of product RC is that of time, so this product is known as time constant

blocks.prompt: 103 The product ohm × farad is equivalent to:
blocks.explanation: RC = (Vt/q)(q/V) = t, so 1 ohm × 1 farad = 1 second (Example 16.9).

book_ref.quote: Verify that an ohm times farad is equivalent to second.

blocks.prompt: 104 A capacitor of 10 μF is charged through a resistor from a 12 V battery. The charge on it after one time constant is:
blocks.explanation: q₀ = CV₀ = 120 μC; after one time constant q = 0.63 q₀ = 75.6 μC (16.8).

book_ref.quote: As the unit of product RC is that of time, so this product is known as time constant

blocks.prompt: 105 A capacitor reaches its equilibrium charge sooner when the time constant is:
blocks.explanation: Fig. 16.12: the charge reaches equilibrium sooner when RC is small (16.8).
